title: Not excusing
hook: forgiving doesn't mean it was okay

segments.voice: Yesterday, not reconciling: Jacob and Esau embraced, wept, and then took two different roads. Your line was from a distance. Did you let go of your end of the rope? Day nine hundred seventy.

"It's fine." Two small words. Someone apologizes for the missed birthday, the sharp comment in the meeting, the promise that quietly fell through, and out comes the reflex: it's fine, don't worry about it, it's nothing. Sometimes that's simply true. Sometimes it's a way to end an awkward moment and get back to dinner. And sometimes it isn't fine at all, and saying so would feel like making a scene. Forgiving someone and telling them it was fine can sound almost the same out loud. Today pulls them apart. Today: not excusing.
screen: `IT'S FINE.` → `SOMETIMES IT ISN'T.` → `TWO THINGS THAT SOUND ALIKE.`

segments.voice: First, the psychologist's list. Robert Enright, a psychologist who has written about forgiveness, sets out what forgiveness is not. It is not condoning. It is not excusing. It is not forgetting. His point is almost a matter of logic: you can only forgive something that was actually wrong. If it was fine, there's nothing to forgive. Second, an old story that does this out loud. In Genesis, Joseph's brothers once sold him away. Years later he has power over them, and after their father dies they're terrified he'll finally take revenge. Listen to the order of what he says: "But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good." Ye thought evil against me. He names it first, plainly, to their faces. He doesn't say it was nothing. Then, in the next verse: "Now therefore fear ye not: I will nourish you, and your little ones." Named, and then let go. Third, why the naming matters. Excusing makes the wrong smaller until it disappears. Forgiving lets the wrong keep its full size, and releases it anyway. That's harder, and it's also more honest, because the person who was hurt doesn't have to pretend. Fourth, what that sounds like on an ordinary Tuesday. Two sentences, both true, said together: that wasn't okay, and I'm letting it go. Neither cancels the other. The first protects the truth. The second frees the one saying it.
screen: `NOT CONDONING, EXCUSING, FORGETTING.` · `YE THOUGHT EVIL AGAINST ME.` · `FULL SIZE, THEN LET GO.` · `TWO TRUE SENTENCES AT ONCE.` · then, large: `IT WASN'T OKAY.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle. Choose one wrong done to you that you've waved away with "it's fine." Now name it clearly, in one sentence, in your head: what they did, and that it wasn't okay. Don't soften it. Don't add a speech. Just the plain sentence. Let it stand there for a few breaths, at its full size. Then, if you're ready, add the second sentence: and I'm letting it go. If you're not ready, the first sentence is enough for today. The bell holds the time.
Not excusing. Forgiving lets a wrong keep its full size and releases it anyway; excusing shrinks it to nothing. Today's word.
Your line: it wasn't okay. Today, the next time "it's fine" is on the tip of your tongue and it isn't, try the honest pair instead, even just in your head. Day nine hundred seventy.

howItsDone: In forgiveness counseling based on Robert Enright's work, people first name the wrong done to them and the harm it caused, and only then consider forgiving; forgiveness is taught as distinct from condoning, excusing or forgetting.

you can only forgive something that was actually wrong. if it was fine, there's nothing to forgive.
Joseph names the wrong before he comforts his brothers
"ye thought evil against me" comes first; "fear ye not" comes after.
on Enright's list, forgetting is part of forgiving
he lists forgetting with condoning and excusing, as things forgiveness is not.

fork.setup: a coworker apologizes for taking credit for your work, and it really wasn't okay. which reply forgives without excusing?
options: "that wasn't okay, and I'm letting it go."
fork.reveal: the honest pair: the wrong keeps its full size, and it's released anyway. Joseph does the same in Genesis 50: "ye thought evil against me," then "fear ye not."

original.note: Hebrew, Genesis 50:20: evil, harm. the word Joseph uses for what his brothers meant against him.

trapdoor: what you thought: forgiving means saying it was fine.
what it means: naming the wrong at its full size, and releasing it anyway.
what a scholar hears: Joseph's order in Genesis 50:20–21, the evil named before the comfort, and Enright's list: not condoning, not excusing, not forgetting.
recall: a poor relative who spread the rumor
